The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with probability kernel $P$, invariant law $\pi$, and natural filtration
$\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. Let $g\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Define
$Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$ and $P(g^2)(x)=\int g(y)^2P(x,dy)$ on the
$\pi$-full measurable set where the respective integrals are finite, and set
these functions to zero on the exceptional set. Then, for each $k\ge0$,
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k).$$
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Consequently, if $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$, then $(D_{k+1})$ is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence and
$$\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with $\mu(X)<\infty$.

1. If $1\le p<r<\infty$ and $f\in\mathcal L^r(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/r}\|f\|_r.$$
2. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $1\le p,q,r\le\infty$ satisfy

$$\frac1r=\frac1p+\frac1q,$$

with the convention $1/\infty=0$. If $f$ and $g$ lie in the corresponding
measurable-function spaces ($\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ or $L^\infty(\mu)$ according to
whether the exponent is finite or infinite), then $fg$ lies in the
corresponding space for $r$ and

$$\|fg\|_r\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

Step 1.1 and bounded conditional multiplication give $\mathbb E[W_K(X_0)f(X_n)]=\pi(W_KP^nf)=\pi(|Z|^p1_{\{|Z|\le K\}})$; since $\pi f=0$, this expectation is the covariance of $W_K(X_0)$ and $f(X_n)$. Bounded conditional multiplication here follows directly from the defining conditional expectation event identity, first for simple $W_K$ and then by uniform bounded approximation. Thus [F1] is applied only to square-integrable variables, even though $p'<2$.

Put $a=\alpha_X(n)$. The quantile identity in [F1] gives $\|Q_{W_K(X_0)}\|_{p'}=\|W_K\|_{p'}$ and $\|Q_{f(X_n)}\|_q=\|f\|_q$. Since $1/p'+1/q=1-\theta$, apply the product inequality [F4] to these two quantile functions in $L^{1/(1-\theta)}(0,1)$, and then Hölder with $1_{(0,a)}$, whose $L^{1/\theta}$ norm is $a^\theta$. Therefore [F1] and step 1.2 give $\pi(|Z|^p1_{\{|Z|\le K\}})\le4a^\theta\|Z\|_p^{p-1}\|f\|_q$. If $a=0$ the quantile integral and the right-hand side are zero. Let $K\to\infty$ using [F6]. If $\|Z\|_p=0$ the required bound is immediate; otherwise divide by $\|Z\|_p^{p-1}$ to obtain $\|P^nf\|_p\le4\alpha_X(n)^\theta\|f\|_q$. The restriction $p<q$ ensures $\theta>0$ and makes all Hölder exponents just used valid.

The geometric bound makes $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_X(n)^\theta\le C^\theta\sum_{n\ge1}r^{n\theta}<\infty$, including $C=0$. By step 2.1, [F4] makes $g_m=\sum_{n=0}^mP^nf$ a Cauchy sequence in $L^p$. Completeness [F5] gives $g_m\to g\in L^p$. The contraction in step 1.1 gives $Pg_m\to Pg$, while $g_m-Pg_m=f-P^{m+1}f\to f$ in $L^p$ by step 2.1. Thus $g-Pg=f$ as almost-everywhere classes. Choose the finite measurable representative supplied by [F5], setting it to zero on its measurable null exceptional set if necessary, and use the version convention from step 1.1 for $Pg$. These choices make the asserted almost-everywhere identity precise on the original sigma-algebra without completing the measure.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose its stationary Markov chain has strong-mixing coefficients $\alpha_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for $n\ge1$, with $0\le C<\infty$ and $0<r<1$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable with $\pi f=0$, $\pi|f|^q<\infty$ for a finite $q>2$, and suppose the absolutely convergent covariance sum is zero:
$$v:=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(f(X_0),f(X_n))=0.$$
Then for every $2<p<q$, under the stationary law,
$$\max_{0\le j\le n}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}f(X_k)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
The empty sum at $j=0$ is zero. No ergodicity assumption is needed beyond the stated stationary mixing bound.

If additionally $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0$ for every $x\in\mathsf X$, the same assertion holds under every initial probability law, without a moment assumption on that law. In particular, it holds under every initial law whenever $P$ has an everywhere finite measurable common geometric total-variation envelope in the sense of [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]] and $f$ has the stated moment, centering and zero covariance sum. No positive one-step minorization, irreducibility or Harris hypothesis is added to this last sufficient condition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the stationary geometric strong-mixing hypotheses, finite centered real $f\in L^q(\pi)$, the zero covariance sum, and any fixed $2<p<q$. For the all-start conclusion assume also the stated pointwise total-variation convergence; for the final sufficient condition assume the everywhere geometric envelope instead.

[A1] AC is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Under the stationary geometric strong-mixing and moment hypotheses, there is a finite measurable $g\in L^p(\pi)$ with $f=g-Pg$ almost everywhere; the covariance series is absolutely convergent and $n^{-1}\mathbb E_\pi(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k))^2\to v$. [[lem-geometric-strong-mixing-gives-lp-poisson-solution]]

[F2] For $g\in L^2(\pi)$, $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$ is square-integrable with $\mathbb E[D_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0$, where $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. [[lem-square-integrable-markov-transition-conditional-expectation]]

[F3] On a probability space $L^p\subset L^2$ for $p>2$; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds products of $L^2$ variables. Conditional expectation preserves means, and a known factor can be taken out when the products are integrable. [[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]], [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]], [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]]

[F4] Monotone convergence passes increasing finite nonnegative sums through expectation; summable event probabilities imply only finitely many occurrences almost surely. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]

[F5] Under AC the canonical Markov path law exists for every initial law. For a bounded product-measurable path functional $H$, $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH(X_0,X_1,\ldots)$ is measurable and $\mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)$. An invariant initial law makes the chain stationary. [[cor-canonical-markov-chain-on-path-space]], [[thm-markov-property-for-bounded-future-path-functionals]], [[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]

[F6] Total variation is $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_A|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$. [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]

[F7] An invariant kernel with an everywhere finite measurable common geometric total-variation envelope admits such an envelope integrable under $\pi$, possibly at a slower geometric rate. That integrable bound implies $\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n$ for the stationary chain. [[lem-harris-geometric-ergodicity-has-integrable-rate-envelope]], [[lem-geometric-total-variation-rate-controls-strong-mixing]], [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to obtain $g\in L^p(\pi)$ with $f=g-Pg$ almost everywhere; choose its finite measurable version as in that supplier. By [F3], $g\in L^2$. Stationarity makes the Poisson identity hold at every $X_k$ simultaneously off a countable union of null events. By [F2], on this common event $f(X_k)=g(X_k)-g(X_{k+1})+D_{k+1}$. Summing gives $S_n:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=R_n+M_n$, with $R_n=g(X_0)-g(X_n)$ and $M_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D_{k+1}$. No ergodic theorem or central limit theorem has been used. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Put $\tau^2=\mathbb E_\pi D_1^2$. Stationarity of transition pairs gives $\mathbb E D_j^2=\tau^2$ for every $j\ge1$. If $i<j$, then $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$-measurable, its product with $D_j$ is integrable by [F3], and [F2]–[F3] give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=\mathbb E[D_i\mathbb E(D_j\mid\mathcal F_{j-1})]=0$. Thus $\mathbb E M_n^2=n\tau^2$. The inequality $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ and stationarity give $\mathbb E R_n^2\le4\|g\|_2^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] and step 1.1 imply $|n^{-1}\mathbb E S_n^2-\tau^2|\le4\|g\|_2^2/n+4\|g\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$. By [F1], the same normalized second moments tend to $v=0$, so $\tau^2=0$. A nonnegative variable of zero expectation is zero almost surely; applying this to each $D_j^2$ and taking the countable intersection shows that all $D_j$ vanish simultaneously. Hence $S_n=g(X_0)-g(X_n)$ for every $n$ on one probability-one event. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Pointwise, the number of positive integers $k$ with $|g(x)|^p>\varepsilon^p k$ is at most $\varepsilon^{-p}|g(x)|^p$. Stationarity and [F4], applied first to finite sums and then to their increasing limit, therefore give $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb P_\pi(|g(X_k)|>\varepsilon k^{1/p})=\sum_{k\ge1}\pi(|g|^p>\varepsilon^p k)\le\varepsilon^{-p}\pi|g|^p<\infty$. Borel–Cantelli [F4], intersected over positive rational $\varepsilon$, yields $g(X_k)=o(k^{1/p})$ almost surely. On that event, for every $\varepsilon>0$ the sufficiently late terms obey $|g(X_k)|\le\varepsilon k^{1/p}\le\varepsilon n^{1/p}$ for $k\le n$, while the maximum of the finitely many earlier terms divided by $n^{1/p}$ tends to zero. Thus $\max_{k\le n}|g(X_k)|=o(n^{1/p})$. Step 1.2 gives $\max_{0\le j\le n}|S_j|\le|g(X_0)|+\max_{j\le n}|g(X_j)|=o(n^{1/p})$, proving the stationary conclusion. [F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For the all-start part, define the original path event $E=\{(x_k)_{k\ge0}:n^{-1/p}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(x_k)\to0\}$. It is product-measurable, since the condition is a countable combination of inequalities for finite measurable sums. It is invariant under deleting the first coordinate: if $s_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(x_k)$, the shifted sum is $s_{n+1}-f(x_0)$, and the reverse identity is $s_n=f(x_0)+(s_n-f(x_0))$ with the second term the shifted sum of length $n-1$. Since $f(x_0)$ is finite and $((n+1)/n)^{1/p}$ and $((n-1)/n)^{1/p}$ tend to one, either normalized convergence implies the other. Iterating gives invariance under deleting any fixed finite prefix. Also, on every real path, $s_n=o(n^{1/p})$ is equivalent to $\max_{j\le n}|s_j|=o(n^{1/p})$: the reverse direction is immediate, and the forward direction follows by discarding a finite initial segment and bounding all later $|s_j|$ by $\varepsilon j^{1/p}$. Thus it suffices to transfer the event $E$, rather than any Poisson identity outside a stationary full-measure set. [given, construct, algebra, step 2.1]

3.2 Let $h(x)=\mathbb P_x(E)$. By [F5], $h$ is measurable and $0\le h\le1$. The canonical stationary chain has the same path law as the stationary chain already considered, so step 2.1 gives $\pi(h)=\mathbb P_\pi(E)=1$; this equality also follows by applying [F5] at time zero and taking expectations. For every state $x$ and integer $n\ge1$, prefix-deletion invariance and [F5] give $h(x)=\mathbb E_x1_E=\mathbb E_x[h(X_n)]=P^nh(x)$. These are identities for each canonical starting state, not simultaneous versions of a conditional expectation over an uncountable family of starts. [A1, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1]

3.3 For any probability measures $\mu,\nu$ and measurable $0\le h\le1$, let $h_m=2^{-m}\sum_{j=1}^{2^m}1_{\{h\ge j2^{-m}\}}$. Then $|h_m-h|\le2^{-m}$ and [F6] gives $|\mu(h_m)-\nu(h_m)|\le\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Letting $m\to\infty$ proves the same bound for $h$. Under the additional pointwise total-variation assumption, apply it to $\mu=P^n(x,\cdot)$ and $\nu=\pi$. Step 3.2 gives $h(x)=P^nh(x)\to\pi(h)=1$ for every $x$, hence $h(x)=1$ everywhere. For any initial law $\mu$, [F5] at time zero gives $\mathbb P_\mu(E)=\int h\,d\mu=1$. The deterministic equivalence in step 3.1 transfers the uniform maximal rate as well. No moment or support condition on $\mu$ is needed. [F5, F6, step 3.1, step 3.2, given, construct]

4.1 Finally suppose the everywhere common geometric bound in the Statement holds. Since its envelope is finite at every state, it implies $P^n(x,\cdot)\to\pi$ in total variation for every $x$. By [F5] the canonical invariant-initial-law chain is stationary. The stronger arbitrary-measurable-space clause of [F7] supplies a finite integrable geometric envelope, and its mixing implication supplies the stationary geometric strong-mixing bound needed by [F1]. Therefore the proof in steps 1.1–3.3 applies to the stated $f$ and zero covariance sum under every initial law. The zero function, a one-state chain, empty partial sums and zero martingale variance are all included; an empty state space admits no invariant probability and does not satisfy the hypotheses. Strict $2<p<q$ is used by [F1] and the $L^2$ comparison. AC is inherited precisely through [F1], [F2], [F3], [F5] and [F7]. This completes both the stationary result and the asserted all-start sufficient conditions. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.3, given] ∎

## Remarks

This is the zero-variance rate only. For a moment $\pi|f|^{2+\delta+\varepsilon}<\infty$ with $\delta,\varepsilon>0$, choose $p$ strictly between $2+\delta$ and $2+\delta+\varepsilon$. The proved $o(n^{1/p})$ rate is stronger than $O(n^{1/(2+\delta)}\log n)$. It therefore supplies the degenerate error estimate needed in a zero-Brownian-coefficient branch without using regeneration, a martingale CLT, KMT, or a nondegenerate SIP. It establishes no positive-variance Brownian coupling.

The Jones and Doukhan–Massart–Rio full PDFs were retrieved, and the source locations specified above were inspected. Their covariance and mixing methods document provenance; the bounded-dual Poisson supplier, zero-martingale variance comparison, integrated-tail rate and deletion-invariant arbitrary-start transfer are all proved locally here or in the explicit mathematical dependencies.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be its stationary Markov chain, and suppose its strong-mixing coefficients satisfy $\alpha_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for $n\ge1$, with $0\le C<\infty$ and $0<r<1$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\pi f=0$ and $\pi|f|^q<\infty$ for some finite $q>2$.

For every $2<p<q$, put $\theta=1/p-1/q$. The kernel operators are understood on $\pi$-almost-everywhere classes, with finite measurable versions obtained by setting divergent integrals to zero on their $\pi$-null exceptional sets. Then
$$\|P^nf\|_{L^p(\pi)}\le4\alpha_X(n)^\theta\|f\|_{L^q(\pi)}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
and the series $g=\sum_{n=0}^\infty P^nf$ converges in $L^p(\pi)$, with
$$f=g-Pg\qquad\pi\text{-almost everywhere}.$$
Moreover, writing $c_n=\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(f(X_0),f(X_n))$, one has
$$|c_n|\le4\alpha_X(n)^{1-2/q}\|f\|_{L^q(\pi)}^2\quad(n\ge1),\qquad\sum_{n\ge1}|c_n|<\infty.$$
The covariance sum $v=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{n\ge1}c_n$ is finite and nonnegative, and
$$\frac1n\mathbb E_\pi\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\right)^2\longrightarrow v.$$

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with probability kernel $P$, invariant law $\pi$, and natural filtration
$\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. Let $g\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Define
$Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$ and $P(g^2)(x)=\int g(y)^2P(x,dy)$ on the
$\pi$-full measurable set where the respective integrals are finite, and set
these functions to zero on the exceptional set. Then, for each $k\ge0$,
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k).$$
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Consequently, if $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$, then $(D_{k+1})$ is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence and
$$\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2\quad\text{a.s.}$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with $\mu(X)<\infty$.

1. If $1\le p<r<\infty$ and $f\in\mathcal L^r(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/r}\|f\|_r.$$
2. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

In fact, the same conclusion holds assuming only AC, invariance of $\pi$, and the everywhere finite measurable common geometric-rate bound in [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]], on the original arbitrary measurable space. The construction below derives the needed irreducibility on a restricted sigma-field directly from that bound.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose there are a measurable
$M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1.$$
Then the strong-mixing coefficient of the stationary process satisfies
$$\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$ on a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$. Write $P^n(x,\cdot)$ for its $n$-step transition probability and use $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ for probability measures.

The chain is **geometrically ergodic** if there are a measurable finite function $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

It is **uniformly ergodic** if this bound holds with $M$ bounded on $\mathsf X$. These are convergence-rate properties, not conclusions about a particular function's CLT or long-run variance. If a proof needs $\int M\,d\pi<\infty$, that integrability is an additional stated hypothesis unless a cited theorem establishes it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to obtain $g\in L^p(\pi)$ with $f=g-Pg$ almost everywhere; choose its finite measurable version as in that supplier. By [F3], $g\in L^2$. Stationarity makes the Poisson identity hold at every $X_k$ simultaneously off a countable union of null events. By [F2], on this common event $f(X_k)=g(X_k)-g(X_{k+1})+D_{k+1}$. Summing gives $S_n:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=R_n+M_n$, with $R_n=g(X_0)-g(X_n)$ and $M_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D_{k+1}$. No ergodic theorem or central limit theorem has been used.

Put $\tau^2=\mathbb E_\pi D_1^2$. Stationarity of transition pairs gives $\mathbb E D_j^2=\tau^2$ for every $j\ge1$. If $i<j$, then $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$-measurable, its product with $D_j$ is integrable by [F3], and [F2]–[F3] give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=\mathbb E[D_i\mathbb E(D_j\mid\mathcal F_{j-1})]=0$. Thus $\mathbb E M_n^2=n\tau^2$. The inequality $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ and stationarity give $\mathbb E R_n^2\le4\|g\|_2^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] and step 1.1 imply $|n^{-1}\mathbb E S_n^2-\tau^2|\le4\|g\|_2^2/n+4\|g\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$. By [F1], the same normalized second moments tend to $v=0$, so $\tau^2=0$. A nonnegative variable of zero expectation is zero almost surely; applying this to each $D_j^2$ and taking the countable intersection shows that all $D_j$ vanish simultaneously. Hence $S_n=g(X_0)-g(X_n)$ for every $n$ on one probability-one event.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Pointwise, the number of positive integers $k$ with $|g(x)|^p>\varepsilon^p k$ is at most $\varepsilon^{-p}|g(x)|^p$. Stationarity and [F4], applied first to finite sums and then to their increasing limit, therefore give $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb P_\pi(|g(X_k)|>\varepsilon k^{1/p})=\sum_{k\ge1}\pi(|g|^p>\varepsilon^p k)\le\varepsilon^{-p}\pi|g|^p<\infty$. Borel–Cantelli [F4], intersected over positive rational $\varepsilon$, yields $g(X_k)=o(k^{1/p})$ almost surely. On that event, for every $\varepsilon>0$ the sufficiently late terms obey $|g(X_k)|\le\varepsilon k^{1/p}\le\varepsilon n^{1/p}$ for $k\le n$, while the maximum of the finitely many earlier terms divided by $n^{1/p}$ tends to zero. Thus $\max_{k\le n}|g(X_k)|=o(n^{1/p})$. Step 1.2 gives $\max_{0\le j\le n}|S_j|\le|g(X_0)|+\max_{j\le n}|g(X_j)|=o(n^{1/p})$, proving the stationary conclusion.

For the all-start part, define the original path event $E=\{(x_k)_{k\ge0}:n^{-1/p}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(x_k)\to0\}$. It is product-measurable, since the condition is a countable combination of inequalities for finite measurable sums. It is invariant under deleting the first coordinate: if $s_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(x_k)$, the shifted sum is $s_{n+1}-f(x_0)$, and the reverse identity is $s_n=f(x_0)+(s_n-f(x_0))$ with the second term the shifted sum of length $n-1$. Since $f(x_0)$ is finite and $((n+1)/n)^{1/p}$ and $((n-1)/n)^{1/p}$ tend to one, either normalized convergence implies the other. Iterating gives invariance under deleting any fixed finite prefix. Also, on every real path, $s_n=o(n^{1/p})$ is equivalent to $\max_{j\le n}|s_j|=o(n^{1/p})$: the reverse direction is immediate, and the forward direction follows by discarding a finite initial segment and bounding all later $|s_j|$ by $\varepsilon j^{1/p}$. Thus it suffices to transfer the event $E$, rather than any Poisson identity outside a stationary full-measure set.

Let $h(x)=\mathbb P_x(E)$. By [F5], $h$ is measurable and $0\le h\le1$. The canonical stationary chain has the same path law as the stationary chain already considered, so step 2.1 gives $\pi(h)=\mathbb P_\pi(E)=1$; this equality also follows by applying [F5] at time zero and taking expectations. For every state $x$ and integer $n\ge1$, prefix-deletion invariance and [F5] give $h(x)=\mathbb E_x1_E=\mathbb E_x[h(X_n)]=P^nh(x)$. These are identities for each canonical starting state, not simultaneous versions of a conditional expectation over an uncountable family of starts.

For any probability measures $\mu,
u$ and measurable $0\le h\le1$, let $h_m=2^{-m}\sum_{j=1}^{2^m}1_{\{h\ge j2^{-m}\}}$. Then $|h_m-h|\le2^{-m}$ and [F6] gives $|\mu(h_m)-
u(h_m)|\le\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Letting $m	o\infty$ proves the same bound for $h$. Under the additional pointwise total-variation assumption, apply it to $\mu=P^n(x,\cdot)$ and $
u=\pi$. Step 3.2 gives $h(x)=P^nh(x)	o\pi(h)=1$ for every $x$, hence $h(x)=1$ everywhere. For any initial law $\mu$, [F5] at time zero gives $\mathbb P_\mu(E)=\int h\,d\mu=1$. The deterministic equivalence in step 3.1 transfers the uniform maximal rate as well. No moment or support condition on $\mu$ is needed.

Finally suppose the everywhere common geometric bound in the Statement holds. Since its envelope is finite at every state, it implies $P^n(x,\cdot)\to\pi$ in total variation for every $x$. By [F5] the canonical invariant-initial-law chain is stationary. The stronger arbitrary-measurable-space clause of [F7] supplies a finite integrable geometric envelope, and its mixing implication supplies the stationary geometric strong-mixing bound needed by [F1]. Therefore the proof in steps 1.1–3.3 applies to the stated $f$ and zero covariance sum under every initial law. The zero function, a one-state chain, empty partial sums and zero martingale variance are all included; an empty state space admits no invariant probability and does not satisfy the hypotheses. Strict $2<p<q$ is used by [F1] and the $L^2$ comparison. AC is inherited precisely through [F1], [F2], [F3], [F5] and [F7]. This completes both the stationary result and the asserted all-start sufficient conditions.

Step 1.2 proves τ²=0 from v=0 using an exact second-moment comparison, then kills every martingale difference on one common event; the zero function is included.
The proof includes n=1, one-state chains, and finite prefix shifts; the n=0 partial sum contributes zero to the maximum.
No ergodic theorem or martingale CLT is used. The endpoint coboundary and Borel–Cantelli proof handle zero variance directly. Arbitrary initial laws require no moments.
p is strictly between 2 and q; Lp embeds in L², while g(Xn)=o(n1/p) uses its actual pth moment. The all-start transfer requires TV convergence at every state, not only π-almost every state.
AC is explicit and inherited through the proved Poisson, conditional-expectation, path-law and geometric-envelope suppliers. No uncountable simultaneous conditional-expectation versions are chosen.
The deterministic equivalence between individual and maximal normalized-sum rates is proved in step 3.1. The theorem itself is not a biconditional.
The reverse direction of that deterministic rate equivalence follows by bounding |S_n| by its partial-sum maximum, explicitly in step 3.1; no converse theorem about zero variance is asserted.

Integrated-tail Borel–Cantelli yields the uniform stationary rate; the measurable prefix-invariant original-path event transfers under everywhere TV convergence. Broad geometric applicability uses the actual strengthened current envelope supplier, with no extra Harris or one-step assumptions.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered square-integrable real random variables. Suppose $b\ge0$ is finite and $|X_i|\le b$ almost surely for each $i$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right|\ge t\right)\le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(v+bt/3)}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then this probability is $0$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: First assume independence and fix positive integers $A$ and $d$ with $d\ge0$. Choose $a$ strictly between $p$ and $q$, put $M_q=\mathbb E|Z_1|^q$, and, for dyadic integers $N=2^m\ge2$, put $b_N=N^{1/a}$, $\ell_N=\log N$, and $r_N=\lceil A N^{1/p}\ell_N^d\rceil$. The second moment $v=\mathbb E Z_1^2$ is finite since $|z|^2\le1+|z|^q$. If $v=0$, the nonnegative variable $Z_1^2$ has zero expectation and is zero almost surely: for each integer $h\ge1$, [F2] bounds $\mathbb P(Z_1^2\ge1/h)$ by zero, and the union of these events is $\{Z_1\ne0\}$. Equality of marginal laws and countable subadditivity make every $Z_k$ zero simultaneously almost surely. This proves the assertion in this case. Henceforth assume $v>0$.

The union bound and [F2] give $\mathbb P(\max_{k\le N}|Z_k|>b_N)\le M_qN^{1-q/a}$. Since $1-q/a<0$, these probabilities are summable over dyadic $N$. By [F3], eventually no one of the first $N$ variables is truncated at level $b_N$, almost surely along the dyadic horizons. Define $m_N=\mathbb E[Z_1\mathbf1_{\{|Z_1|\le b_N\}}]$ and $V_{N,k}=Z_k\mathbf1_{\{|Z_k|\le b_N\}}-m_N$. For each fixed $N$, these variables are independent and centered, $|V_{N,k}|\le2b_N$, and $\operatorname{Var}(V_{N,k})\le v$. Moreover centering of $Z_1$ gives $|m_N|\le\mathbb E[|Z_1|\mathbf1_{\{|Z_1|>b_N\}}]\le M_qb_N^{1-q}$.

For an interval of at most $r_N$ indices, [F1] bounds the tail of its $V_{N,k}$ sum by $2\exp(-x^2/[2(vr_N+2b_Nx/3)])$; if its actual variance is zero the bound still holds because the tail is zero. Set $x_N=C(\sqrt{r_N\ell_N}+b_N\ell_N)$, where $C\ge\max\{\sqrt{20v},40/3,1\}$. Then $2vr_N\le x_N^2/(10\ell_N)$ and $4b_Nx_N/3\le x_N^2/(10\ell_N)$, so the bound is at most $2e^{-5\ell_N}=2N^{-5}$. There are at most $N^2$ intervals with integer endpoints in $[0,N]$. The probability that any interval of length at most $r_N$ violates the bound $x_N$ is therefore at most $2N^{-3}$, summable over dyadic $N$. By [F3], all such interval sums are bounded by $x_N$ eventually almost surely.

On the eventual no-truncation event from step 1.2, every original interval sum differs from its centered truncated sum by at most $r_N|m_N|$. Now $\sqrt{r_N\ell_N}=o(N^{1/p})$ because $1/(2p)<1/p$, and $b_N\ell_N=o(N^{1/p})$ because $1/a<1/p$. Also $r_N|m_N|\le M_qr_NN^{(1-q)/a}=o(N^{1/p})$. Thus step 2.1 proves the claimed little-o bound at dyadic horizons. These comparisons follow by dividing by $N^{1/p}$: in each expression a strictly negative power of $N$ multiplies a fixed power of $\log N$, which tends to zero.

For $2^{m-1}<n\le2^m=N$, monotonicity of $n^{1/p}(\log n)^d$ gives $r_n\le r_N$, so every admissible interval for $n$ is included among those for $N$. Since $N^{1/p}\le2^{1/p}n^{1/p}$, step 2.2 proves the assertion at every horizon $n$. Intersect the probability-one events obtained for the countably many integer pairs $A\ge1,d\ge0$. For arbitrary real $A>0,d\ge0$, choose integers $A'\ge A$ and $d'\ge d$; when $n\ge3$, $\log n\ge1$ makes the real-parameter window no longer than the integer-parameter window. The conclusion therefore holds on one event for every $A,d$ in the Statement.

Under one-dependence, each parity subsequence is independent. Indeed, the sigma-algebra of any finite initial collection of even variables is contained in $\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{2h})$, which is independent of $Z_{2h+2}$ by the given separation; induction on the number of factors proves the finite rectangle factorization for all even variables. The identical argument applies to the odd variables. Both subsequences retain the common centered marginal and its $q$th moment. Apply step 3.1 to each subsequence and intersect their two probability-one events. An interval of at most $r_n$ original indices splits into one contiguous interval of each parity, each with at most $r_n$ terms and with its subsequence endpoints at most $n$. Each component is $o(n^{1/p})$ by the independent result, uniformly over the original intervals; their sum has the same bound. No independence between the parity subsequences is asserted or needed. All windows are nonempty by $i<j$; empty component windows contribute zero. This completes both dependence cases, including zero variance and every permitted window parameter.

Independent parity subsequences need not be independent of each other; step 4.1 uses only the triangle inequality between them.

No converse or necessity of the moment condition is asserted.
